print(s.find("o"), t.find("o"))

options.rationale: find() on s still counts the two leading spaces, because strip() returned a new string and left s unchanged.
t has no leading spaces, so its first "o" is two positions earlier.
In s the first "o" is at index 6 (after two spaces and "Hell"); in t it is at index 4.
This swaps the two results: s is the string that still has the leading spaces.

explanation: find() returns the index of the first match. In s, the two leading spaces take indexes 0 and 1, so "Hello" starts at 2 and its "o" is at 6. strip() and lower() return a new string "hello world", where the "o" is at 4. The original s is not changed.

stem: Which expressions evaluate to the string `"tea"`? (Select THREE)

options.rationale: `strip()` with no argument removes all whitespace from both ends, including the new line.
`lower()` makes every letter small.
Replacing every dash with an empty string removes the dashes.
`rstrip("!a")` removes any `!` or `a` from the right end, so the `a` of `tea` goes too, leaving `"te"`.
`capitalize()` keeps the first character capital, so this gives `"Tea"`.
`lstrip()` trims only the left end, so the trailing space stays: `"tea "`.

explanation: `strip()` removes whitespace (spaces, tabs, new lines) from both ends, `lower()` makes every letter small, and `replace("-", "")` deletes every dash. `rstrip("!a")` treats its argument as a set of characters, so it also eats the final `a`. `capitalize()` leaves a capital `T`, and `lstrip()` keeps the space on the right.
